This was at a time when white performers were doing all the voices. If there was a black character on the screen a white actor was voicing him. If there was a song made famous by a black musician, then the toons used a white cover. The Fleischer brothers were the first ones to celebrate black jazz makers on screen. Cab Colloway, Louis Armstrong and others were seen by general audiences for the first time working these cartoons. If the stereotypes were easier to draw (like women with big breast were easier) then that happened. But this was the first time white kids were seeing and hearing these

Another wonderful effort from the Fleischers highlighting and featuring early black jazz/pop music performers, here featuring Louis Armstrong and His Band. Yes, the African natives are portrayed in the style of the day - but ,sad to say, stereotypes still exist. Otherwise early Armstrong on film is historically significant. It may irk some, but I really wish they had used Cab Calloway rather than Armstrong. But that's life. A great cartoon.
Betty Boop cartoon or Louis Armstrong video?

A Betty Boop adventure set to Louis Armstrong sound track, and there can´t be that much film still existing of Louis Armstrong performing from this time. So definitely worth coming here to watch because it´s most unlikely to get a TV airing. This and a few other BB cartoons do reflect 1930´s racial attitudes and right or wrong, its important to keep them on record. (And some things haven´t changed that much, black and white popular music still tends to be segregated, you will find "Black music" filed in separate racks in many record shops).

It's a great song. It's hard to watch though, because of the way they juxtapose Louis Armstrong and his Orchestra with such racial stereotypes. rv: Part 9 of Ivan Besse's late 1930's film of Britton,South Dakota

Watching this film makes me almost feel I am getting to know the people of Britton during the late 1930's. It is interesting watching them doing their routines on the main street, and seeing the various events they went to. It looks like they enjoyed their life. This silent film certainly captures a bygone American way of life. I wish there could have been some sound narration, but at that time it would have been very expensive to make.

This bears a suspicious resemblance to the Simpsons parody "The World Without Zinc"--all that's missing is Troy McClure. Gilbert, frustrated with sofa seat repair, wishes springs out of the world. Evil animated Coily-the-spring grants the wish and keeps popping up worse than a Microsoft paper clip. It isn't really a problem for Gilbert until he can't drive his Chevrolet for lack of springs. When Coily pops up, Gilbert wishes his wish away, and in return becomes a scientician orating about springs. Especially those that produce the smooth ride of a modern motorcar, which he is fortunate enough not to have his pals drive over him in order to demonstrate.

rv: Edgar Ullner is at it again with the TB films.. This time it's a children's film about it! The film opens up with a dad and their two kids, the kids want to know what Dad is reading, and the dad, who repetitiously keeps poking junior in the stomach with his pipe, says it's about TB! The kids say wouldnt it be great if the TB germ could talk, and dad says "yessssss..." and from there of course, we're in fantasy land where a scientist, who has FAR too many animals in his lab, talks to a TB germ (actually animated of course). Pretty engaging, and for sure will keep the kids entertained.

Most of this info is still pretty valid. The film itself is very stilted and awkward. The doctor character is rather creepy in a sweet sort of way. Probably not the guy you'd want to leave your children with for any extended period of time. I like old films like this- They show where we were at and help us to understand how we got to here. So, in conclusion, educational, a bit weird, and definitely one for the vaults.
